_comment: Real plants, with an append-only status history. This is the file the watch agent's
second channel writes to, and the reason its shape is strict.
Schema and vocabularies: sources/sector_map.py. Gate: sources/check_sector_schema.py.
STATUS_HISTORY IS APPEND-ONLY AND EVERY ENTRY CARRIES A SOURCE. A status that changed
without a link is a status nobody can check, and the history is the one part of this
layer that is meant to be read as a record rather than as an analysis. Entries are in
date order and the last one equals `status`; the gate fails on either being untrue,
because a header and a timeline that disagree put two different facts on one page.
A SHORT HISTORY IS HONEST. Several of these projects start their history at the event
this repository first sourced — the grant, the groundbreaking — rather than at their
announcement, because no primary source for the earlier event has been read yet. The
file records what was verified, not what is likely to have happened.
`public_funding.measure` points at the register measure that IS the programme, and carries
`measure_note` saying how tight the fit is. The Innovation Fund lines are the live case: the
grants were awarded under the Fund as it stands (Art. 10a(8) of the ETS Directive), while the
register knows the Fund through the revision's Art. 10cb, which re-establishes it. Linking them
is what lets the money model total public support for the sector; the note is what stops the
link from being read as a claim that the award was made under the proposed article.

`public_funding` used to sit on each row. It moved to data/transition/funding.json, where capital allocation is a node with edges out of it: one Innovation Fund call finances several projects, and a field on the recipient could only say so by repeating itself once per recipient. The project keeps a rollup and the rollup is DERIVED — computed from the funding rows wherever it is shown, never stored back here.
`shared`: OPTIONAL, AND ONLY EVER TRUE. A project is claimed by the ecosystem whose
product it makes (page specifications §4.2), and two claims on one project fail the
build — a boundary drawn twice is a boundary somebody has to redraw. A CO2 store or a
hydrogen pipeline serving three industries is the exception the rule needs, and it
says so with "shared": true and a note giving the industries it serves. A plant making
one product never carries it.
WHERE IT IS, IN THE SAME BREATH AS WHAT IT IS. `location` is a LIST of sites, because a
project is not always at one place: the ArcelorMittal row covers Bremen and
Eisenhüttenstadt, and a single point for it would put a fact on the map that is half
wrong. One site is the ordinary case and the list of one says so honestly.
Every site carries {site, lat, lon, precision, retrieved_date, source, confidence} — the
parameter discipline, applied to a coordinate. `precision` is `plant` for a works and
`site` for a store or a terminal; `town` is in the vocabulary only so that the gate can
name what it is refusing. A town centroid is not a plant location: it would draw a mark
a reader would take for the works, several kilometres from the works. The coordinates
are read off OpenStreetMap features that carry the operator's or the works' own name,
which is a source that states a position rather than an address somebody geocoded in
their head; where a company publishes the plant address, `address` records it beside the
point. `confidence` is `secondary` throughout: OpenStreetMap is a third party reporting
somebody else's site.
`role` says what kind of place it is, and the map draws each differently. `plant` is the
default and is omitted; `storage` is a permitted or proposed geological store. A store is
in this file rather than in one of its own because it is what this file already says it
is — a real installation with an append-only status history — and because the exception
the `shared` flag was written for is exactly a CO2 store serving several industries.
`storage` IS REQUIRED ON EVERY CAPTURE PROJECT and has two shapes. Either it names the
project id of the store the tonne reaches, with the source that names it; or it says
`"unresolved": true` with a note saying how far the chain is actually specified. Five of
the nine capture projects here are unresolved, and that is the finding, not a hole: a
kiln with a capture unit and nowhere to send the CO2 is the thing the sector page exists
to show. An unresolved row still carries a source, because "nobody has said" is itself a
claim about a document somebody read.

AWARD TERMINATED. The Innovation Fund's own project factsheet for grant 101085967 — 'ANRAV-CCUS' — carries the word TERMINATED twice over an award of 'EUR 189,694,949' to DEVNYA CEMENT AD, and states 'FINANCIAL CLOSE DATE 30 September, 2026' and 'ENTRY INTO OPERATION DATE 31 October, 2029'. The funder is the speaker and this is money leaving the project. THE DATE IS AN UPPER BOUND: the fiche says 'Updated on 09 September 2026' and gives no date for the termination. THE STATUS DOES NOT MOVE and an owner look is queued. D-B19, applied.

owner_look.why: A FUNDER HAS SPOKEN AND THE OWNER HAS NOT. Rule 17's narrow task: read whether the owner's own source still stands — not whether the project stopped. No status moves on it.

urls.note: Devnya Cement AD is the beneficiary the funder names. Its own site is where a statement about the ANRAV award ending would appear. FIRST READ 20 September 2026: 200, 5522 chars.

Heidelberg Materials owns Devnya Cement; the group's own site is the second place to look. /en/press answered 404 on 20 September 2026, so the queue carries the root. FIRST READ 20 September 2026: 200, 11499 chars.

status_history.note: A FIRST PARTIAL PERMIT UNDER THE BImSchG, and the status does not move: a permit is permission to build, not building. The Landesamt für Umwelt is the licensing authority and its procedure G10/2023/091 — 'Neubau einer Anlage zur Herstellung von Lithium-Ionen-Akkumulatoren (Batteriezellenfertigungsanlage Northvolt DREI)' — names the applicant as Northvolt Drei Project GmbH and the site as Blauer Lappen 2, Lohe-Rickelshof, Gemarkung Rickelshof, Flur 1, with its parcels listed; the portal shows public participation running 20 April to 4 June 2026. THE GRANT ITSELF IS REPORTED AND NOT PUBLISHED WHERE THIS PIPELINE CAN READ IT: trade press dated the first partial permit 10 April 2026, alongside a €153 million repayment on the convertible bond to the federal and state governments, and the LfU's own press index carries no release for it. The date is the reported one and the source is the authority's file on the procedure.

Lyten signed an exclusive memorandum of understanding with KfW, Northvolt Drei Project GmbH and its shareholder LG Batterie GmbH to progress an acquisition of the assets. The 110-hectare site has groundwork and utilities in place, with 15 GWh under construction and plans to scale beyond 30 GWh. A memorandum is not a completed sale, so the owner is unchanged here and no ownership event is recorded. The state's own release of the same week says the same thing from the other side: the parties will sign an exclusive letter of intent, it is 'rechtlich noch unverbindlich', and binding contracts are to be drafted and signed at a later 'closing'. REPORTED AND NOT RECORDED AS A FACT: Lyten's chief executive is said to have told the state government in March 2026 that construction would start in 2027 and production in 2028. No state or company page carrying that timetable could be read here — the ministry's and the Staatskanzlei's own releases do not state it, the trade reports of it are behind a consent wall or a 403 — so it is named as reported and no date on this row rests on it.

The January 2021 Commission decision the FY2020 10-K points at is the second battery IPCEI, 'European Battery Innovation' (IP/21/226, 26 January 2021, German case SA.55831). It is now on file as funding germany-ipcei-tesla-gruenheide. Read in full: it states no capacity in GWh for any site, and its text does not name Tesla at all — the 42 participants are listed only in a graphic. Brandenburg's two ministry releases, which do name Tesla and Grünheide, state no capacity either. So there is no `official`-basis figure to record and the row stays empty. The remaining official document that could carry one is the non-confidential version of the decision in the State Aid Register under SA.55831, which the Commission said would follow; it has not been read here.

source.note: THE PLAN NAMES THE PARCELS AND THE STATE CADASTRE HOLDS THEIR GEOMETRY, which is what the `plan_parcels` source type is: two documents doing one job, neither of them able to place anything alone. The point is the area-weighted centroid of the two put together — the same construction as Sunderland's, where the permit listed emission points and the centroid of those was the works. 57 of the 58 parcels the Begründung lists as wholly inside the Geltungsbereich were found in Gemarkung Überherrn, Flur 1 and Flur 3, in the Saarland INSPIRE cadastral service (LVGL, dl-de/by-2-0); 152/11 was not, and four labels occur in both Fluren and are both counted, which moves the point by tens of metres. THE CANCELLATION IS THE AUTHORITY'S OWN, not press. The Überherrn council resolved on 7 May 2026 to repeal the plan, and the notice says why: 'Gegenstand der Aufhebung ist der Vorhabenbezogene Bebauungsplan „Industriegebiet Linsler Feld“, der die planungsrechtlichen Voraussetzungen für die Ansiedlung einer Batteriezellfabrik schaffen sollte. The repeal Begründung records the mechanism: gwSaar, the Vorhabenträger that had bought the land to grant SVOLT a heritable building right, declared it would not hold to the project, which triggers the municipality's duty to repeal under § 12 Abs. 6 BauGB. SVOLT's European withdrawal was reported earlier in trade press and no company statement of it has been read here, so the date this row carries is the authority's.

The repeal notice says 'Das Vorhaben wird nicht mehr umgesetzt' and the Begründung gives the mechanism — gwSaar declared it would not hold to the project, which triggers the municipality's duty to repeal under § 12 Abs. 6 BauGB — and neither is a reason. THE STATUS DOES NOT MOVE — a funder withdrawing its money is a fact about the award, and reading a cancellation out of it would be this register deciding something the owner has not said. RWE says both halves of it in one release. 'As part of the ongoing commissioning process for two 100-megawatt electrolysis plants operated by RWE in Lingen, initial quantities of renewable hydrogen are being produced in accordance with EU rules' — and 'We are now moving ahead quickly towards the full commissioning of our electrolysers. RECORDED AS `construction` UNTIL 9 SEPTEMBER 2026, WHEN THE LADDER GREW A RUNG. THIS EVENT COULD NOT BE FILED UNTIL 9 SEPTEMBER 2026, and the reason is worth keeping. galp.com renders its publication dates in the browser, so the company's own FID release came back to a declared reader with its text and no date — and an undated statement cannot date an event. The history therefore began at the EIB's release of 29 September 2025, with a construction event and a lender for a source, and the row said so. What changed is not the evidence but the schema: an event date may now carry year precision, padded to 1 January, with the precision recorded. 'The two projects, already in construction at the Sines Refinery, represent a total investment of €650 million.' THE SOURCE TYPE IS THE NEAREST FIT AND NOT A GOOD ONE: the European Investment Bank is a lender publishing a financing decision, and this vocabulary has no value for a lender — `grant_register` is the closest, `regulator` would say the EIB acted on the project, and `official_register` would say the state wrote down a fact. The gap is on the docket as a candidate class for a later ruling. IT IS NO LONGER THE FIRST ENTRY. Until 9 September 2026 this was where the history began, because Galp's own FID release carries no date a declared reader can read; the company's project page dates the decision to 2023 and now carries it, at year precision. The Innovation Fund's own project factsheet for grant 101179454 carries the word TERMINATED twice — once under the project title and once beside the participant — over an award of 'EUR 230,463,819' to a '500 Megawatt electric' electrolyser, and states 'FINANCIAL CLOSE 31 December, 2025' and 'ENTRY INTO OPERATION DATE 31 December, 2028'. The fiche says 'Updated on 09 September 2026' and gives no date for the termination itself, so the event is `not_after` that day: it happened at or before then and nobody here knows when. THE STATUS DOES NOT MOVE. The row stays `announced` because that is where the OWNER's own statement leaves it, and a funder withdrawing its money is a fact about the award, not about what the company says it is building. owner_look.why: RULE 17'S SHAPE, APPLIED TO A FUNDER RATHER THAN TO A LIST. A project that vanishes from a database is a project whose failure nobody counts, so the register goes and looks — and what it looks at is whether the OWNER's source still stands, not whether the project stopped. A terminated award is the same shape one step over: it is evidence about the award, and the owner has not spoken. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT is a statement by Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, Enagas Renovable, Naturgy, Fertiberia or Vestas about Project Catalina, or by the grant coordinator CI ETF I Renato Ptx Holdco S.L.U. projects.location_note: POSITION OUTSTANDING, AND THE ADDRESS IS ON FILE RATHER THAN DRAWN. UniverCell publishes 'Unser Standort: Konrad-Zuse-Ring 1, 24220 Flintbek, Deutschland' on its own company page, in the same paragraph as the sentence that says it operates the works — which is the Iváncsa case and not the Giga Arctic one: the address is presented as the address OF the works, not as a filing address. What it is not is a coordinate, and this register does not geocode. The drawing is queued: a sweep centred on Flintbek against a dated extract is what turns the address into a position citing the feature it came from. Recorded here so the absence is a decision and nobody repeats the reasoning.
projects.capacity_note: THE COMPANY'S OWN FIGURE, AND IT IS A FLOOR RATHER THAN A TARGET. UniverCell's company page says the works is 'bereit, über 1,5 GWh hinaus zu skalieren' and its home page states '1,5 GWh verfügbare Kapazität'. 1.5 GWh is therefore capacity available now, not capacity announced for a future phase, which is why the basis is `operating` and not `announced`. Battery-News.de's February 2026 atlas states 10 GWh for this works against a 2026 date; that figure is the second list's and is recorded as a disagreement in sources/batteries_benchmark.json rather than blended into this one.

status_history.note: THE HISTORY STARTS HERE BECAUSE THIS IS THE FIRST EVENT ON THIS WORKS THIS REGISTER HAS SOURCED, and the date is the day the statement was read rather than the day production began. UniverCell's company page carries no dateline, on the page or in its markup, so the day it was read is an upper bound on when the company said it: 'jetzt betreiben wir eine erfolgreiche Gigafactory, die bereit ist, über 1,5 GWh hinaus zu skalieren'. The home page carries the same claim as 'die größte aktive Gigafactory Europas'. NOTHING EARLIER IS READ IN. The works is older than this sentence and this register has read no primary source for when it started, so it records what it verified.

Once operational, the unit will capture over 95% of the site's emissions - equivalent to more than 800,000 tonnes of CO2 annually.” THE OWNER STATES A LOWER BOUND, NOT A POINT VALUE (D84). Converting a bound into the number that satisfies it would invent precision and make this register's figure look like an independent reading of the list's.
